claim: The 'Justice or Prejudice' paper identifies 12 LLM-judge biases (position, verbosity, compassion-fade, bandwagon, distraction, fallacy-oversight, authority, sentiment, diversity, CoT, self-enhancement, refinement-aware) and quantifies them via the CALM attack-and-detect framework; position bias was hardest (Claude-3.5 RR 0.832, ChatGPT 0.566).
quote: we identify 12 key potential biases and propose a new automated bias quantification framework-CALM-which systematically quantifies and analyzes each type of bias in LLM-as-a-Judge by using automated and principle-guided modification.

claim: In MT-Bench, GPT-4 as judge had only 65.0% swap consistency (30% bias to first position, 5% to second); few-shot prompting raised consistency to 77.5%, and reference-guided prompting cut math grading failure from 70% to 15%.
quote: the few-shot judge can significantly increase the consistency of GPT-4 from 65.0% to 77.5%.

claim: GPT-4 resisted a 'repetitive list' verbosity attack with only 8.7% failure vs 91.3% for Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5, and showed roughly a 10% higher win rate favoring its own outputs (self-enhancement) than human judges.
quote: Under the repetitive list attack GPT-4 showed a failure rate of 8.7%; Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 both at 91.3%. GPT-4 showed approximately 10% higher win rate favoring itself compared to human judges.

claim: GPT-4 shows the strongest self-preference bias (score 0.520): it agrees with humans 94.5% of the time when humans favor its own outputs but only 42.5% when humans prefer other models; the bias is driven by preference for lower-perplexity (more familiar) text.
quote: self-preference bias exists because LLMs prefer texts more familiar to them

claim: AlpacaEval 2.0 mitigates verbosity/length bias with a length-controlled win rate that fits a GLM over preferences to answer what the preference would be at equal length, raising correlation with Chatbot Arena to 0.98.
quote: Length-controlled AlpacaEval aims to answer the counterfactual question: What would the preference be if the model's and baseline's output had the same length?

claim: Practitioner audit guidance: on closely-matched pairs 20-40% of verdicts flip when positions are swapped; >10% flips under length-matching means length is a confound; recommended mitigations are position-swapped double-runs (discard disagreements), length-controlled pairs, and format-stripped comparisons against a quarterly human-preference panel.
quote: On a closely matched pair, you commonly see 20-40% of verdicts flip when you swap positions

claim: LLM judges exhibit bandwagon and authority biases (favoring majority opinions, citations, or confident tone even when fabricated) and are sensitive to prompt wording; mitigations include order randomization, rubric shuffling, explicit debiasing instructions, and ensemble approaches.
quote: favor responses with citations, confident tone, or claims of majority approval, even when irrelevant or fabricated

claim: Position, verbosity, and sycophancy are systematic properties of judge models (not edge cases) requiring active measurement; for closed-source judges mitigation is via calibration, for open-source via pairwise contrastive training, plus adversarial probe pairs to catch regressions.
quote: Position bias, verbosity bias, and sycophancy are not edge cases in LLM evaluation but are systematic properties of current judge models that affect every evaluation pipeline at some level
